source_text: Amici mei et proximi mei adversum me appropinquaverunt et steterunt. Fidelis infirmus mugit pro delictis; conscientia accusatrix mecum est — cur exspecto accusatorem?
thought_title: Friends and neighbors stand against me; conscience as accuser
orientation: Origen is interpreting Psalm 37 (LXX 36), where the psalmist speaks of his suffering under sin and the weight of guilt.
pass_a_gloss: Friends my and neighbors my against me drew near and stood. [The] faithful [one] weak groans for [his] offenses; [the] conscience accusing with me is — why [do] I wait for [an] accuser?

choices.english: drew near against me and stood
choices.why: Keeps the physical motion and hostile stance of the psalm verse, preserving the sequence of approach and standing.
rejected: came near me and stood against me
approached me and took their stand

choices.why: Renders both adjectives as descriptive of the same person, preserving the psalmist's self-description as faithful yet weak.
Captures the low, animal-like sound of deep distress implied by the Latin verb, fitting the psalm's lament.

choices.english: the accusing conscience is with me
choices.why: Keeps the personified conscience as an accuser standing with the speaker, matching the brief's description of conscience as an accuser.

choices.english: why do I wait for an accuser?
choices.why: Preserves the rhetorical question and the first-person present tense, conveying the futility of waiting for an external accuser when conscience already accuses.
rejected: why should I wait for an accuser?
why am I waiting for an accuser?

bible_refs.note: amici mei et proximi mei adversum me appropinquaverunt et steterunt

pass_b_english: My friends and my neighbors drew near against me and stood (Psalm 38:11 (LXX 37:11)). The faithful one, weak, groans over his offenses; the accusing conscience is with me—why do I wait for an accuser?
